\newcommand{\trivial}{trivial monitoring}
\newcommand{\Turing}{Involved interaction}
\newcommand{\Many}{Endpoint action}
\newcommand{\Trivial}{Trivial monitoring}


\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
The legal compliance and safety of different Human-in-the-loop (HITL) setups for AI can vary greatly. This manuscript aims to identify new ways of choosing between such setups, and shows that there is an unavoidable trade-off between the attribution of legal responsibility and the technical explainability of AI. We begin by using the notion of oracle machines from computability theory to formalise different HITL setups, distinguishing between trivial human monitoring, single endpoint human action, and highly involved interaction between the human(s) and the AI. These correspond to total functions, many-one reductions, and Turing reductions respectively. A taxonomy categorising HITL failure modes is then presented, highlighting the limitations on what any HITL setup can actually achieve. Our approach then identifies oversights from UK and EU legal frameworks, which focus on certain HITL setups which may not always achieve the desired ethical, legal, and sociotechnical outcomes. We suggest areas where the law should recognise the effectiveness of different HITL setups and assign responsibility in these contexts, avoiding unnecessary and unproductive human ``scapegoating''. Overall, we show how HITL setups involve many technical design decisions, and can be prone to failures which are often out of the humans' control. This opens up a new analytic perspective on the challenges arising in the creation of HITL setups, helping inform AI developers and lawmakers on designing HITL to better achieve their desired outcomes.
\end{abstract}


\section{Introduction}

Human-in-the-loop (HITL)---the practice of embedding human oversight directly into AI decision-making processes---is frequently invoked as a safeguard to ensure AI systems' safety and accountability~\cite{Green.2022}. Yet, as we show, the effectiveness of HITL for satisfying both safety and regulatory requirements hinges critically on the specifics of the system's design and implementation. Different setups exist and can lead to vastly different outcomes, ranging from \textit{trivial monitoring}, to a single \textit{endpoint action}, and to \textit{involved interaction} (we define these formally in the section \textit{HITL as a computational reduction}). Existing legal frameworks, such as Article 22 of~\citet{GDPR.27.04.2016} and Article 14 of~\citet{EUAIAct.12.07.2024} only partially consider HITL, and do not account for the variety of setups possible. In this manuscript, we  formalise the notion of a HITL as a computational reduction (focusing on many-one and Turing reductions), and clarify the various outcomes, failure modes, and legal and moral responsibilities associated with each. We further argue for an inherent tension present within all HITL setups: increasing human interpretability and explainability of HITL systems hinders clear attribution of responsibility, and vice versa. 

Although introducing a HITL is increasingly a strategic choice to improve sociotechnical systems~\cite{Grnsund.2020}, our focus is not on optimising the average-case performance, but rather on ensuring safety, reliability, and robustness. We are primarily concerned with preventing AI-related harms, by recognising that different degrees of human involvement in HITL setups carry varied technical and ethical implications that should be recognised by the law. Our perspective therefore asks when a HITL represents genuine and meaningful human control of AI systems, and encompasses its moral, legal and political ideals of keeping ``social control'' over technology~\cite{Abbink.2024}. The questions guiding this manuscript are therefore normative: when, if ever, should we use HITL? And how can we select HITL setups in order to minimise harm and risk? (cf.~Pillar 1 in~\cite{chiodo2023manifestoresponsibledevelopmentmathematical})

Our primary contributions are threefold. First we present a novel formalisation of different categorisations of HITL setups as different types of computational reductions. Second, we highlight a selection of failure modes and ethical considerations for different HITL setups. And finally, we consider what HITL setups the law requires and how responsibility is assigned when they fail. In doing so, we contextualise the failure models and categories of HITL setups to highlight ways laws can be improved to ensure safety and efficacy. We also uncover an unavoidable trade-off between responsibility and explainability in HITL setups.


\subsection{Existing terminology}

The existing terminology describing human involvement with AI systems varies with differing degrees of human interaction and control. HITL setups have humans actively integrated into the AI's operational cycle, while Human-on-the-loop (HOTL) have humans primarily acting as supervisors who intervene only when necessary~\cite{nothwang2016human}. Setups where the AI is designed to operate without direct human input or intervention can be termed Human-out-of-the-loop (HOOTL)~\cite{wagner2011taking}. A higher level perspective is given by Human-in-Command (HIC), whereby humans determine the high-level functioning of the AI~\cite{anderson2022human, kowald2024establishing}. To bridge the legal and ethical responsibility gaps~\cite{matthias2004responsibility} that can exist in such setups, the concept of Meaningful Human Control was introduced to study how much influence a human should have on the execution of an action and what necessary levels of cognitive and moral awareness they should possess~\cite{davidovic2023purpose, roff2016meaningful, Abbink.2024}. In this context, \citet{Green.2022} speaks of three human oversight policies: 1) ``restricting solely automated decisions'', 
2) ``emphasising human discretion'', 3) ``requiring meaningful human input.'' Later, we show how existing HITL terminology can be understood from the perspective of formal computability theory, and use this to deconstruct (3) above into a more fine-grained categorisation.


\subsection{Existing conceptions of HITL}

HITL setups can in certain situations mimic the trolley problem (i.e., a HITL needing to choose between multiple undesirable outcomes), particularly when the HITL has no ability to shut off the AI entirely, but often also go beyond it in legal, moral and technical complexity~\cite[cf. ][]{Steenson.2021}. Recent research suggests that while HITL approaches lead to more uptake of AI, they potentially also decrease accuracy~\cite{sele2024putting}. \citet{Green.2022} particularly discusses the empirical evidence for human oversight policies of AI, arguing that these generally fail to address the fundamental flaws in controversial government algorithms while simultaneously offering legitimisation of the algorithms and the protection of vendors and agencies from accountability. \citet{Elish.2019} similarly raises the point that HITL setups can end up protecting the AI rather than the human, speaking of humans as the ``moral crumple zone'' taking on accountability and enabling potentially faulty AIs to stay in place. Overall, this literature suggests that a closer scrutiny of HITL setups and their failure modes is necessary. 

The lack of a well-defined meaning of what a HITL can and does involve, and why HITLs may be beneficial in AI sociotechnical systems, is a recognised problem. Recent literature has attempted to specify potentially desirable setups of HITL in medical contexts. \citet{co-reasoners} have argued that both clinicians and patients should be included as ``co-reasoners'' in a medical AI context, making their own judgments about if, how, and why to use this technology, as well as how to use its results. Accordingly, they argue that such a HITL setup is valuable in that it forces questioning by both parties about whether to use AI technology thereby justifying its use, reduces automation bias by encouraging doctors to not rely on AI without justifying its use to the patient, and uses AI not just as a tool to generate answers but as ``discussion'' prompts based on the values and aims of both patients and doctors.  Building off Eriksen and Salloch's setup, \citet{griffen2024human} have argued for a kind of proliferation of HITLs in medical AI systems, highlighting the potential role of other clinical staff, and the value of having a diverse range of HITLs.

Recognising that human experts must play an active role in HITL setups, \citet{natarajan2025human} argue to shift the perspective and call such systems AI-in-the Loop (AI$^2$L), whereby it's the AI  that is part of a larger sociotechnical (human-led) process. Recognising the different degrees to which humans are, and should be, involved in producing functioning HITL setups, we present a classification of these (using Turing and many-one reductions) to concretise the language for further legal and ethical analysis. 

HITL is frequently presented as a critical safety measure in high-risk domains~\cite{EUAIAct.12.07.2024}, such as autonomous driving~\cite{Huang_2024} and the military~\cite{HITL_in_military}. However, the scalability of human oversight has been increasingly questioned~\cite[cf. ][]{chiodo2024regulating}, especially for advanced AI models. The challenge of \textit{scalable oversight} highlights fundamental limitations: human supervisors may struggle to meaningfully oversee AI systems whose cognitive capabilities surpass their own across multiple domains~\cite{amodei2016concreteproblemsaisafety, bowman2022measuringprogressscalableoversight}. Our work in this manuscript, on both the formal classification of HITL setups, and their failure modes, will help shed light on the positive and negative safety aspects of different HITL setups.


\subsection{Author contribution}

The first author (Chiodo) led the project. Authors 2-5 (Müller, Siewert, Wetherall, Yasmine) are listed alphabetically by surname, and all contributed equally. The final author (Burden) oversaw the project. All authors contributed to drafting, writing, and editing. 


\section{Computational Reductions for HITL}

\subsection{Abstract oracle machines} 

An \textbf{oracle machine} is a deterministic automaton $T^\bullet$ with a normal work tape, an extra `oracle tape', and some states marked as `oracle states'. For any function $f$ from words to words, $T^\bullet$ gives rise to a `machine with oracle' $T^f$, whose computations proceed as usual, but which whenever it enters an oracle state has the content $w$ of the oracle tape (instantly) replaced by $f(w)$. This definition is reminiscent of the notion of $\exists$-non-determinism and random automata, in that $T^\bullet$ by itself defines, for any input, a computation tree that contains all possible behaviours depending on the behaviour in the oracle states (respectively, the non-deterministic states or the random states). The difference is in semantics, as the result of one computation is not defined by some general property of the computation tree, but by `plugging in' $f$ and thus resolving all the choices with $f$. A full discussion of oracle machines can be found in~\cite[Chapter III, Section 1]{soare87}; we have adopted here a slight variation of the terminology from~\cite[Section 2.4]{melkebeek}. 
 
Depending on how $T^\bullet$ relies on its oracle, the computational power of $T^f$ may be drastically different even for the same $f$. The most salient distinction in the context of HITL is that between machines which only call $f$ once, and those which call $f$ an unbounded number of times. We should remark these correspond to two different notions of `reduction' between functions $f$ and $g$: if there is an oracle machine $T^\bullet$ such that $T^f$ computes $g$, one says $g$ is \textbf{Turing-reducible} to $f$. If moreover $T^\bullet$ is such that it halts immediately after its first call of the oracle (with output the oracle tape), then one says $g$ is \textbf{many-one reducible} to $f$. 

Another, more basic point is that an oracle call may be rather trivial. For instance, it could be that $T^\bullet$ completely ignores the content of the oracle tape, in which case the choice of $f$ does not matter. Even if $T^\bullet$ does write to and read from the oracle tape, it may be that its computational result does not actually depend on these steps. However, our concern lies with the \textit{function} defined by $T^{f}$, not the machine itself\footnote{One could examine it to increase computational transparency.}. Therefore, we are interested more so in what we define as a \textbf{real query}, which we say occurs at an oracle call if a fork exists at that point in the computation tree \textit{and} there are $>1$ different computational outputs the machine could produce after that query. The former of these is to ensure that the oracle can still have some meaningful impact on the computation, and the latter is to ensure that we avoid an ``all roads lead to Rome'' scenario where the algorithm can take multiple computational paths all leading to the same output. 


\subsection{HITL as a computational reduction}

We propose describing human-AI systems in terms of this formalism. Any human-AI computational process is (perhaps implicitly so) designed in a way to use algorithmic components at some points and human interventions at others. We hence conceive of a HITL setup as a type of Human-Based Computation~\cite{HBComp}, in the sense that the AI assigns particular tasks or problems to a human to solve. Our perspective though is quite different to how the term is typically used. First we are not so much interested in large-scale human knowledge, but more so in the specialised knowledge that individuals possess. And second, the human is not the subordinate labourer of the AI or a simple assistant, but rather is in symbiosis with the entire system. We now examine this to see what sort of computational reliance on, or use of, human inputs the machine can have.

The architecture of a decision-making process including the algorithmic specifications corresponds to the oracle machine $T^\bullet$. The function $f$ is provided by the HITL: at certain points in the decision process, human judgment on values and data enters the computation, which corresponds to $T^\bullet$ calling the oracle, and which we denote as a \textbf{human query}. With this notion we include human interventions that are otherwise uninvited by the algorithm; computationally, it makes no difference what precipitated the human input\footnote{In reality, this still needs to be considered for evaluating safety.}. In response to a human query, we allow the human to write an ``emergency stop'' symbol to the oracle tape, denoted by \textbf{!}; whenever the machine reads ! on the tape it halts immediately with no output\footnote{Thus, not needing to separately define ``human stops machine''.}. Note that the possibility to halt after a query with no output does not count towards the number of computational outcomes when determining if a query is real.

If an oracle machine is set up to never ask a human query, and humans have no way to intervene in the operation of the machine, this corresponds to a HOOTL system as explained above, and we will not cover this further here.

If an oracle machine is set up to ask human queries, but none are real queries, then we denote this by saying there is a \textbf{human trivially monitoring the loop}, abbreviated to \textbf{\trivial}. This corresponds to a HOTL system as explained above, but where the human is only able to stop the process. Computationally, in a \trivial{} setup, the  human is not affecting the computational steps of the machine in any meaningful way, and serves only to prevent the machine from reaching the end of its computation\footnote{A potential crucial safety role as argued by~\citet[p. 448]{Crootof.2023} when discussing human sign-off requirements by ``positioning human(s) as end-of-the-loop gatekeepers''.}. This means that $T^\bullet$ defines a total function, independent of the human oracle, whereas the only thing the human can decide is whether to terminate the algorithm before it completes its computation (an ``ignorance is bliss''-scenario).

If an oracle machine is set up to ask precisely one real human query and then immediately halt giving the answer to that real query as its output, then we denote this by saying there is a \textbf{human at the end of the loop}, abbreviated to \textbf{\many}. Here, the machine does some computation, and then hands over to the human to perform the rest of the computation.

If the oracle machine is set up to ask more than one, and potentially an unbounded number of, real queries (i.e., a number not a priori bounded before the algorithm starts its computation), we denote this by saying there is a \textbf{human involved in the loop}, abbreviated to \textbf{\turing}. Practically, this is most resembling the scenario of human and machine working together. In an \turing{} setup, the machine engages the human in a game of computational ping-pong: the machine does some work, then hands it over to the human to do some, who then hands back to the machine, and so forth, to-and-fro. One example of this is a ``creative'' collaboration with a Large Language Model (LLM). A human might give an LLM a prompt, the LLM may use that and produce an initial response (or ask a question), then the human uses that to determine the next piece of information they give the LLM (e.g., ``do more'', ``use green instead'', ``correct fact X  to fact Y'', etc), and so on, to-and-fro.

Thus, our definition of an \textit{\turing{}} means the oracle machine Turing-reduces the computation to the human oracle, but \textit{does not} many-one reduce it. Our definition of an \textit{\many{}} means the oracle machine many-one reduces the computation to the human oracle, but it \textit{does not} define a total function on its own. And our definition of \textit{\trivial{}}  means the human oracle can terminate the machine, but not otherwise influence its computation.


\subsection{Why are we considering these reductions?}

In computer science, a Turing reduction between functions is viewed as weaker than a many-one reduction, as many-one implies Turing. This comes from a viewpoint that \textit{fixes a computational problem}, and then asks what the space of oracles it reduces to is. So a Turing reduction is considered weak, because the problem reduces to more oracles; a many-one reduction would reduce it to fewer oracles so the reduction itself is strong. Thus, if one tries to many-one reduce a given problem to some oracle rather than Turing-reduce it, then one (generally) requires a stronger oracle, which in the context of HITL setups means a more competent human. Therefore, our concern is the opposite: we advocate maximising the space of functions that can be computed with a \textit{fixed oracle} (a human). With that perspective, a Turing reduction is considered strong, because there are more problems that reduce to the given oracle than if we used many-one reductions instead. In a HITL setup, the oracle is fixed (the human), so limiting the setups to \many{}s limits the space of problems that can be solved. Therefore, making the space of problems solvable as large as possible is achieved by maximising the influence of the human.

But why do we want this? Because human (oracle) influence can add valuable, desirable insights to the overall computation, with benefits such as the following: 

Firstly, the human has more influence on the overall computational process, and thus on the outcome. With more, potentially unbounded, real human queries, the \textit{agency} of the human is increased. Secondly, and related to this, the human has more opportunity to input their judgements and values into the overall computational process, thus giving more opportunity for the human to ensure the AI computation is \textit{aligned} with its values.

Thirdly, by intervening more often, the human has more opportunity to identify (and rectify) problems and safety issues within the AI computational process, before a final output or behaviour occurs. Increased human queries `bakes in' the potential for increased human scrutiny. This aids with the \textit{safety} of the HITL setup. Finally, and related to this, with more human queries, the AI is articulating intermediate steps that are human-interpretable more often (as a human input is sought), thus aiding with \textit{transparency} of the  computational process. Overall, these four aspects come together to improve the \textit{reliability} of the HITL setup.

Therefore, we propose that the HITL setups with the greatest potential to achieve agency, alignment, safety, transparency, and thus overall reliability, are those with the greatest reliance on human input (i.e.,  \turing{}s).

There is however a ``computational trade-off'' in increasing human involvement: more powerful reductions (i.e., Turing) are necessarily less predictable than weaker ones (i.e., many-one). This is because of the increased indeterminism in the computation tree; with a Turing reduction, there is more branching as there are more (potential) calls of the oracle. But predictability of what \textit{will} happen in the computation is the same as explainability of what \textit{has} happened. This trade-off between predictability and power corresponds to trade-offs between explainability and responsibility explored later. 


\subsection{Examples of our HITL types}

How might we see practical examples of this? Consider an algorithm providing route-planning assistance to the human driver of a car:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{\Trivial{}:} The human could enter the origin and destination, and the algorithm could then present a driving route. The human then has the choice to take the route, or not. Here, the human has no input to the calculation process, and can only ``turn off'' the algorithm (by ignoring its output).
    \item \textit{\Many{}:} The human could enter the origin and destination, and the algorithm could present the human with several different options, perhaps labelling them as ``fastest'', ``most fuel efficient'', ``most reliable'', ``passes fuel stations regularly''.  The human can then choose between these. Here, the human takes over at the end of the machine's work to finish the calculation.
    \item \textit{\Turing{}:} The human could instead input into the algorithm ``I want to visit my sibling''. The algorithm could then start computing, and asking the human a series of questions such as ``when are you travelling?'', ``when do you need to be there by?'', ``what do you need to bring?'', ``is anyone else travelling with you?''. The algorithm \textit{may} then present some sort of optimised driving route. Or it may produce a very different output, such as suggesting to take the train as there is bad traffic, or to go on another day  closer to the sibling's birthday. Or it may even advise against travel due to adverse weather. Here, the human has regular, meaningful, and not a priori bounded input into the calculation.
\end{itemize}

These examples demonstrate the full (computational) spectrum of HITL setups, from \trivial{} (where the human simply has to accept or reject the suggested route), to \many{} (where the human takes over at the end to choose their preferred route), to \turing{} (where the human is fully involved in the suggestion process, from the early formulation stage right up to the latter optimisation stage). Note that with growing reliance of the procedure on human queries, the agency of the human and the access of the algorithm to human values increases, resulting in decisions becoming more adjusted to the human needs.

\subsection{HITL setups in existing work}

The more real queries  involved in the computation, the more a human that is part of the process appears as a HITL, rather than a HOTL in the sense laid out above. \citet{Adersen2024Design} describe a set of 10 \textit{design patterns} for HITL. Three of these are centred around HITL during deployment/inference. The first of these is the ``Recommendation System'' where a human operator is ultimately making the final decision based on the output of the machine. The second is ``Active Moderation'' where, for a set of tasks, humans perform the task in the cases where the AI system cannot do so reliably. The third option ``Thumbs up or Thumbs down'' sees the human overseer either accept or correct an AI system's output. All of these can be seen as either an \many{}, or \trivial{}. Notably, none of~\citet{Adersen2024Design}'s patterns describe interactions where the task is aborted rather than corrected---effectively requiring the human to be as capable as the AI at the initial task (rather than being able to ``merely'' recognise an error). Later, we will discuss the relation to Meaningful Human Control.


\subsection{Intermediate HITL setups}

So why have we omitted denoting restricted cases of \turing{}, such as where the machine can only ask the human oracle a bounded finite number of real queries (corresponding to a Turing reduction where the oracle can be consulted only a bounded number of times)? Computationally, this would be stronger than a many-one reduction, but weaker than a Turing reduction (see below). The reason is that we do not wish to consider all intermediate reduction types between many-one and Turing\footnote{Including bounded truth-table reductions, truth-table reductions, and weak truth-table / bounded Turing reductions. See~\cite[p. 83]{soare87} or~\cite[Section 2.4]{melkebeek} for details.}. Conceptually, an \many{} describes the ``simplest'' way a human can interact with a machine in a computationally meaningful way, and an \turing{} describes the ``most complicated''; these two types alone give us a deep and rich area to analyse. It may well prove valuable to replicate the technical, legal, and moral analysis done in this manuscript on some of these intermediate reductions (e.g., when the machine can do its calculation, hand over to the human to do some more, then take back the human output and do some final machine calculation; having ``one round of ping-pong''). The technical, legal, and moral possibilities may well be endless, so we have elected to examine the extremal cases for now: \many{}s, and \turing{}s, as defined above.  


\subsection{Complicated HITL \many{}s}

Despite the restriction in our scope outlined above, we shall briefly consider  one distinction. This naturally arises from a sociotechnical observation about the examples given earlier of a HITL setup providing route-planning. In the second scenario, describing an \many{}, the algorithm could have instead asked the human a fixed finite series of questions such as 1) Do you prefer the fastest or most fuel efficient route?, 2) What is your maximum acceptable distance between fuel stations?, etc., and done some computation between each. This would almost appear to be an \turing{}. However, these could be encapsulated by instead asking the human to chose an option from a (longer) list presented at the end.

This corresponds to a type of intermediate reduction as mentioned earlier (a bounded truth table reduction). It is not a ``full'' Turing reduction because an oracle machine for which the size of the computation tree is bounded independently from the oracle and that uses the tape content only a computable number of times which is independent from its oracle function $f$ is easily replaced by an oracle machine that calls a slightly different function only once and then performs a trivial operation. Namely, an oracle machine that asks a (human) oracle a (predetermined, finite) set of questions ``in series'' one after the other, is computationally equivalent to one which does a slightly different computation with these options ``in parallel'' and presents the conglomeration of questions to the oracle at the very end, phrased as one (big) question. So essentially these setups are the same as those which have only one real query, which are slightly stronger\footnote{The Halting-problem does not many-one reduce to its complement, but there is a Turing reduction with only one query. It remains to be discussed when this distinction matters for human oracles.} than those for \many{}, but weaker than those in \turing{}.

Note however that although this sketch describes a \emph{computational} equivalence, there is a big difference in practical terms between asking a human a sequence of, say, 20 binary questions, and presenting them with $2^{20}$ options to choose from; the latter being completely unmanageable for a human. Thus, as covered in the next section, computational aspects are not the only thing to consider in HITL setups; the abilities and limitations of the humans must also be factored in, as humans do not behave like abstract oracles. But, if we are to properly understand how human input feeds into a HITL setup, and ``design out'' some of the failure modes presented in the next section, then we must first understand how the human is involved from a computational perspective.


\subsection{Determining HITL types in practice}

It now becomes an interesting question to ask: how does one identify when a HITL setup is \trivial{}, \many{}, or \turing{}? This is interesting from technical, legal, and moral perspectives.

From a technical perspective, showing the non-existence of a reduction is difficult. While it is fairly straightforward to show the existence of, say, a many-one reduction, by simply constructing such a reduction, that would not (in our terminology above) show that a HITL setup is an \many{}. To achieve that, one would also need to show that the machine was not total, and that it always asks a real human query during the computation. Similarly, to show a HITL setup is an \turing{}, one would need to show a Turing reduction, and also show that the machine always asks more that one real human query during the computation. Heuristically, while it is ``easy'' to show that there is a human in the loop, it is much harder to show how much the human will actually be asked to do, reflecting the computational trade-off mentioned above.

From a legal perspective, showing the human will do something meaningful is also difficult. One could have a HITL setup where there are real human queries, but these are completely deterministic and replicable by the  machine (i.e., asking the human ``What is 1+1?''). Asking the human a series of ``pointless'' questions (that the machine could just as easily carry out itself) may violate the legal principles of ``meaningful'' or ``effective'' human input, as discussed later. 

From a moral perspective, showing the HITL setup is not simply a facade masking a less-involved process is also difficult. One could have a HITL setup where there are real human queries which the machine cannot do itself (i.e., bringing in genuine human judgement), but then the remainder of the (machine) computation simply ignores the input. Asking the human a question with a (seemingly) important answer, and then not using that, would at best be a terrible oversight by the AI developers, and at worst be completely disingenuous and unethical of them.

Overall, the classification of HITL types into \trivial{}, \many{}, and \turing{} outlines what is \textit{possible} with HITL setups. But auditing such setups, from the technical, legal, and moral perspectives given above, is a very different problem. While we have provided a technical definition of HITL setups which is both robust and useful, specifying genuine computational reductions, practically verifying these is another challenge altogether.


\section{HITL Failure Modes}

\subsection{Characteristics of effective HITL setups}

According to~\citet{10.1145/3630106.3659051}, necessary and sufficient conditions for effective (general) oversight of AI are given when the human overseer has 1) an adequate understanding of the system, 2) the self-control to act on their judgment, 3) the power to intervene effectively, and 4) intentions aligned with the oversight goals. They and other researchers note that successful oversight depends on many user-specific attributes, including technical skills, domain knowledge, general attitudes towards technology, especially those related to interpreting the AI's outputs, as well as attributes of the human-machine setup~\cite[cf. ][]{10.1145/3630106.3659051, Sudeeptha.etal.2024, langer2025test}. The arguments presented in the literature remain at a comparatively abstract level, and do not distinguish by HITL type. Overall, as our reductions make clear, the functioning of HITL setups does not rely on the design of the AI alone, nor just on the characteristics of the human overseer, but on how they are put into relation with each other.  This complex sociotechnical relationship sets the basis from which one can turn the theoretical and empirical insights from the literature into practice, and analyse potential failure modes. 

\subsection{Taxonomy of HITL failure modes}

We now present our own taxonomy centred around five main failure categories, giving a partial breakdown of each:


\subsubsection{1. Failure of the AI components}\mbox{}

$\bullet$ Unexpected inputs or outputs

$\bullet$ Problematic evolution or self-adaptation of the AI

$\bullet$
Other unexpected AI behaviour 


\subsubsection{2. Failure of the process and workflow}\mbox{}

$\bullet$  Insufficient power of the human

$\bullet$  Insufficient self-control/independence

$\bullet$  Insufficient reaction time

$\bullet$  Unrealistic expectations

$\bullet$  Delayed notification

$\bullet$  Insufficient support


\subsubsection{3. Failure at the human-machine interface}\mbox{}

$\bullet$ Incomprehensible or incomplete outputs

$\bullet$ Complex or poorly designed user interface

$\bullet$ Insufficient training

$\bullet$ Other epistemic failures


\subsubsection{4. Failure of the human component}\mbox{}

$\bullet$ Cognitive bias

$\bullet$ Automation bias

$\bullet$ Fatigue

$\bullet$ Incongruous intentions

$\bullet$ Stress or overload

$\bullet$ Lacking courage


\subsubsection{5. Exogenous circumstances}
\mbox{}

$\bullet$ Unreasonable laws

$\bullet$ Unreasonable societal expectations

$\bullet$ Other external pressures

\medskip

These categories represent general themes in the literature on HITL failures, and are closely connected to our reductions from before. The list is ordered by ``amount of human-ness present'', starting with failure of purely digital components (no human-ness), and ending with failure of social pressure and wider society (vast human-ness). 


\subsection{Connections to our HITL setup types}

Systems configured for \trivial{}, where the human cannot provide computationally meaningful input beyond ``proceed'' or ``halt'', may be particularly susceptible to failure modes related to the human component. The human's comparatively passive role means that automation bias, fatigue, or simply lacking the courage or perceived authority to halt a process become significant risks. This setup can also mask process and workflow design failures, such as the human having insufficient power to truly intervene or having unrealistic expectations about the level of oversight provided. Failures originating in the AI components themselves might also proceed unchecked, as the monitoring human lacks the mechanism or mandate for closer scrutiny.

When there is \many{}, the system relies on a single, critical human input after the AI has performed its computation, concentrating failure risks around that specific interaction point. Human-machine interface failures become critical: if the AI presents incomprehensible or incomplete outputs, or if the interface is poorly designed, the human may be unable to make informed decisions. Similarly, human component failures like cognitive bias can influence their single judgment with no backup checks present. Failures in process and workflow design, such as insufficient reaction time allowed for the human or delayed notification that input is required, are also highly relevant here.

In setups where a human is in an \turing{} with potentially many stages, failure modes quickly become more complex. The back-and-forth nature of the process makes larger design failures (e.g., unclear roles) and human-machine interface issues more pronounced. While increased interaction might help the human to catch AI failures (and indeed vice-versa), it could also lead to unexpected AI behaviour if the AI adapts to the user in unintended ways. Human failures such as fatigue or stress due to prolonged interaction, or the accumulation of cognitive biases across multiple decision points, can additionally degrade performance over time. Furthermore, the complexity involved can hide superficial engagement with the AI outputs when quantitative interaction is mistakenly understood as qualitative interaction: many smaller human-AI interactions may not sufficiently change the AI's output. Overall, while a HITL setup requiring \turing{} gives the human the most power to intervene, it is also the setup which is most complex, thus leading to more nuanced failure mechanisms.

In summary, different failure categories may be more likely for different HITL setups, and each category can be realised through different failure modes. We believe this taxonomy of five failure categories is able to capture \textit{most} HITL failures. However, the list below each category should not be seen as exhaustive, but rather reflects a selection from the wider literature.\footnote{For example, \citet{10.1145/3630106.3659051} develops a taxonomy for general human oversight; while only considering technical design, human, and environment, they discuss many of the individual failure modes. See also~\citet{Green.2022} for governmental decisions, \citet{Bainbridge1983} for automation of industrial processes, \citet{endsley1995toward} for situational awareness, \citet{Sarter.1997} for automation surprises, or~\citet{reason1990human} for human errors and ``Swiss Cheese Models''~\cite{larouzee2020good}.} They are here to illustrate that one should not only consider HITL setups via reductions, but also by simultaneously grouping different failure mechanisms into different categories. This provides a two-dimensional actionable picture of HITL setups focused on harm prevention. Ignoring entire categories is likely a sure way to failure, and ignoring items on the list will probably also lead to some sort of failure. In short, reductions and failure categories should always be considered together.


\subsection{Examples of HITL setup failures}

To show this taxonomy is not purely hypothetical, we now apply it to several case studies of (failed) HITL setups, showing where and why these systems failed, in relation to the above taxonomy. What comes to light from these is that failures of HITL setups are usually due to poor integration~\cite[cf. ][]{muller2025integrators}, and what is often put down to ``technical failure'' or ``human error'' can actually be avoided if proper integration is carried out.


\subsubsection{AI security scanners:} As presented in~\cite{Robertsonetal.2025}, in April 2025 two men were alleged to have brought firearms though the AI-powered security scanning system at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG). This was an \many{} HITL setup, with AI scanners used to flag attendees who \textit{might} be carrying weapons, and then manual secondary screening used to conduct a final, definitive inspection. Initially, the  blame was conjectured to have been ``human error'' in the secondary scanning process.  However, as mentioned in (ibid.), with a potentially high false-positive rate, secondary (human) scanners may have faced the combined challenges of operator fatigue (having to scan many attendees in a short space of time as they arrived for the beginning of a match), as well as complacency (having to scan countless attendees, \textit{none} of whom were actually carrying weapons). The human scanners may have become quite tired, and many have lost faith in the AI scanner as it overwhelmingly returned false positives.


\subsubsection{Semi-automated fire detection systems:} As presented in~\cite{BennholdGlanz.07.05.2025, Peltier.18.06.2019}, in April 2019 a catastrophic fire broke out in the attic space of Notre Dame Cathedral. The cathedral had an \many{} HITL fire monitoring setup.\footnote{This was not an AI system, but nonetheless was a HITL machine setup that failed completely with spectacular consequences.} When a fire was detected by the machine, a short message ``fire'' was sent to the monitoring office in the cathedral, without specifying exactly where the fire was (incomplete outputs). As is standard across France, fire alarms never automatically notify the fire brigade, so as to avoid false callouts (unreasonable laws). The employee on duty was only on his third day of the job and working unsupervised (insufficient training, unrealistic expectations). The employee was required to phone a guard, who  then had to physically check the attic; a 6 minute journey up many stairs (insufficient reaction time). Unfortunately, the guard got lost, and went up the wrong staircase to the attic of the sacristy, which was the adjacent building (insufficient training). The employee then called his manager rather than the fire brigade (lacking courage), but could not reach him (insufficient support, insufficient power of the human), and it took time for the manager to call back and instruct the guard to leave the sacristy, go down the stairs, and then climb another staircase to the attic of the cathedral. By the time the guard reached the attic of the cathedral, the fire was raging. The fire brigade was then called, over 30 minutes after the first detection of a fire.


\subsubsection{Self-driving cars:} As presented in~\cite{Hawkins.2018, Fitzsimmons.2018, NationalTransportationBoard.2019}, in March 2018 the first recorded incident of a pedestrian fatality from a collision with a self-driving car occurred. The car had a \trivial{} HITL setup created by Uber, with a human driver (an Uber employee) at the wheel poised to intervene and ``take over'' the driving at any point if they observed a problem with the self-driving mechanism~\cite[p. 8]{NationalTransportationBoard.2019}. In this HITL setup, the human operator monitored the AI responsible for autonomous driving and had the ability to intervene by breaking and/or taking the wheel, but they did not have the ability to change the AI's decision-making in more complex ways. The human monitor was expected to perpetually ``hover their hands above the steering wheel and foot above the break pedal'' (ibid., p. 12) (unrealistic expectations), without ever touching them as that would disable the self-driving system (ibid., p. 11). The car had been in self-driving mode for 19 minutes before the crash, with no tasks required of the human driver (ibid., p. 19) (fatigue, automation bias). The self-driving system first identified the pedestrian 5.6 seconds before collision, as they were jaywalking across the road. However, as it had not been programmed to classify a jaywalker (ibid., p. 16), it spent the next 4.1 seconds misclassifying the pedestrian as ``another vehicle'', ``bicycle'', and ``other'' (ibid., p. 15) (unexpected inputs). The system first predicted a collision 1.5 seconds before impact and began evasive action; at 0.2 seconds before impact the system established that impact was inevitable, instigated a controlled slowdown, and gave the human driver the first warning notification of upcoming impact (ibid., p. 16) (delayed notification, insufficient reaction time). The human driver had, from 6 seconds before impact, been gazing down at the control panel (ibid., p. 18), allegedly watching their cellphone (ibid., p. 24) (incongruous intention). With a warning lead-in time of 0.2 seconds, which is approximately human reaction time, the human driver had virtually no time to take control; they took the wheel 0.02 seconds before impact, and the car then hit the pedestrian. The entire HITL setup was affected by a poor safety culture (ibid., p. 38) (insufficient support, other external pressures).

The failure cascade spans across our taxonomy: (1) the AI components failed by not recognising the pedestrian, (2) the workflow failed as the human allegedly was not embedded in a supporting safety-culture and had insufficient reaction time and unrealistic expectations, (3) the human-machine interface setup failed by allowing an environment whereby the human could watch a video, and (4) the human failed by being inattentive. However, there was one key further failure of this system, post-incident, which was that the laws failed to hold the company accountable in any way or form (corresponding to (5) from our taxonomy), which brings us the final aspect of our manuscript: responsibility.


\section{Legal-Moral Responsibility}

If a HITL setup fails and causes harm, the law questions what went wrong and who is at fault. The previous Uber case study sheds light on the challenges when legal frameworks intersect with HITL failure modes. In this case, both criminal and civil liability fell on the Uber \textit{employee} who was operating the car. Uber was absolved of all legal liability, even though its technology was allegedly flawed (i.e., not recognising the jaywalking pedestrian) and the company's safety culture was evidenced as poor~\cite[for full details of the case, see][]{stamp2024reckless}. In the final section of this manuscript, we consider relevant (EU, UK) legal frameworks concerning design setups and failure liability and point to ways that they can be improved by incorporating our formalisation of HITL setups. We also identify a trade-off between \turing{} and legal clarity, but prompt the courts to consider more nuanced approaches in these instances so HITL are not treated as default `scapegoats' (like in the Uber case). 


\subsection{Responsibility for the design of HITL setups}

Both the UK and EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)\footnote{The GDPR only applies where the automated decisions involve the processing of personal data (Article 4(1) GDPR).} and the EU AI Act have imposed requirements for human oversight mechanisms to be implemented for automated decision making systems and high-risk AI systems\footnote{AI systems are considered `high-risk' if they meet the description of the AI systems covered in Annex III of the EU AI Act.}. Both legal frameworks take a `by design' approach, requiring developers to embed certain safety mechanisms into the technical setup of their AI systems. This means that the law does not only give a threat of legal liability when things go wrong (which is discussed in the next section), but also mandates measures to \textit{prevent} harm from occurring in the first place. Given the scope of the GDPR and EU AI Act in relation to HITL, law makers have acknowledged that HITLs are most important to prevent harm in high-stakes scenarios like biometrics, law enforcement, and employment (\citealp[Annex III]{EUAIAct.12.07.2024} and~\citealp[Article 22(1)]{GDPR.27.04.2016}).


\subsection{The law focuses on trivial monitoring HITL setups} 

Under Article 22(1) of the GDPR, `solely automated decisions' are generally prohibited where they could cause legal effects (or similar) on individuals, such as in the context of online credit applications or e-recruiting practices~\cite[Recital 71, GDPR]{Vollmer.2023}. In the SCHUFA case, the~\citet{EuropeanCourtofJustice.07.12.2023} established that where a lender relied heavily on the credit score provided by an agency, this amounted to a `solely automated decision' because the lender's HITL did not consider any other data relevant to determine creditworthiness. Thus in the context of our HITL types, even though it \textit{appeared} as though there was an \many{} setup, the HITL only looked at the credit score; a process that is easily automated, turning it into \trivial{}. Following this case, GDPR guidelines require companies to implement `meaningful oversight' to prevent \trivial{} and comply with Article 22~\cite[p. 19]{EuropeanCommission.2018}.

The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to be ``designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which the AI system is in use''~\cite[Article 14(1)]{EUAIAct.12.07.2024}. The wording from both legal frameworks (`effective' and `meaningful') indicate that \trivial{} is not enough to prevent harm from AI systems. A human presence at the final stage of processing with no actual influence on the decision or computation cannot be doing anything meaningful or effective. But, the law (and associated guidelines) do not indicate what alternative HITL setups should be implemented to meet these obligations set out in Article 14 of the EU AI Act and Article 22 of the GDPR. 


\subsection{Requiring human \turing{}}

Current laws focus on the role of humans at a very late stage in the HITL setup. As~\citet[p. 4]{sarra2024artificial} notes, ``substantial human intervention in previous stages appears to be irrelevant''. There are computational and ethical implications where human interventions occur earlier in the process. As discussed previously, where humans have a greater influence on the computational process, this increases the potential for more human-aligned, safe, transparent, and reliable AI systems. Only focusing on what a HITL can do when the possibilities do not extend to altering the computational processes neglects the beneficial influences of a HITL in \many{} and \turing{} setups.

We suggest that, beyond requiring that humans have some form of oversight or control over the final decision (something more than \trivial{} in high-stakes or automated contexts), the law should place greater responsibilities for companies to design systems in ways which enable \many{} (as an absolute minimum), and ideally \turing{}. \Turing{} enables the possibility of unbounded querying of the HITL, as opposed to them just being in a position to `turn off' the algorithm when they might suspect a fault, or taking the output of the algorithm and making the ``final call'' on what to do (like in the SCHUFA case). So by designing an \turing{}, the HITL will be better positioned to make `meaningful' and `effective' interventions to prevent failures in line with Article 14 of the EU AI Act and Article 22 of the GDPR.


\subsection{HITLs as superhuman legal safeguarders}

Here, we focus on HITL responsibility in the event of \textit{failures}. The GDPR and EU AI Act place responsibilities on companies (data controllers or technology providers) to safeguard decision subjects from harm. Article 14(2) of the EU AI Act requires that human oversight should ``prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights'' that may emerge from high-risk AI systems. Similarly, Article 22(3) of the GDPR requires that measures, such as human intervention mechanisms, are implemented to ``safeguard the data subject’s rights and freedoms and legitimate interests''. Here, we see a paradox: these are high expectations to place on a HITL, especially when it's unclear how the system's setup can even enable them to perform these `safeguarding' functions.\footnote{\citet{Green.2022} also comments on the lack of empirical evidence demonstrating that a HITL can even protect these values.} Given the limited design requirements, a HITL may have to be \textit{superhuman} to meet these legal obligations.

In \trivial{} and \many{} setups, the HITL is unlikely to have any understanding of whether `fundamental rights' or `legitimate interests' are being infringed. They may have no influence on, or understanding of, the computational process involved in the decision. Indeed, the HITL may face a completely ``black box output''. For example, in an \many{}, the HITL may just receive a probability score for credit risk. Using only this, the HITL would need to determine whether it should be applied to an individual and also whether it infringes any values. Thus, \many{} and \trivial{} setups contain an inherent opaqueness which prevents  HITLs from understanding the significance of certain inputs or factors on the output of the system. As a result, HITLs may lack sufficient knowledge and ability to influence, effectively evaluate, and implement the decisions made by an AI in line with their duty as legal safeguarders.

In contrast, in \turing{} setups, HITLs are more effectively integrated into the process, enabling them to make inputs that actually change the computational path of the system. This places the HITL in a far better position to safeguard rights by directly inputting their knowledge of the sociotechnical system and its potential impacts on individuals. Extending the credit scoring example above, the HITL could be asked questions like `is the individual's postcode relevant to the credit score?' or `what information should be used to substitute the lack of credit history?'. Additionally, \turing{} setups give the HITL a chance to watch and scrutinise more of the computational process, as mentioned earlier. This may help overall safety, as they may ``spot a problem'' early on, such as the AI asking questions about a credit applicant that should not be used as part of the assessment. Therefore, \turing{} avoids the `sloppy'~\cite[p. 434]{Crootof.2023} implementation of a HITL into these setups, by enabling HITLs to better evaluate the output of an AI in accordance with the rights and freedoms of decision subjects. 

From a legal perspective, this is significant because the better a developer or company can ensure that the HITL can meet their obligations, the more they can reduce their own risk of liability. It should be noted however that \turing{}s are not inherently better in \textit{all} possible contexts, and designing systems in these ways will not prevent failures from ever arising. \Turing{}s are still subject to all the potential HITL failure modes mentioned previously, and this should be accounted for in their design.


\subsection{HITL responsibility and explainability trade-off}

However, while an \turing{} may enable a HITL to positively impact, and understand, the output of an AI, this comes with a trade-off which fundamentally complicates the issue of explainability, and by extension, legal and moral responsibility. 

In the literature on AI technology and moral responsibility, ``responsibility gaps'' refer to situations where the so-called ``black box'' features of autonomous technologies, combined with the complexity of the sociotechnical system, obfuscates an immediate source of responsibility for the impact of an AI (assisted) decision~\cite{matthias2004responsibility}. Ironically, introducing HITLs into AI systems has been posited as a way of narrowing responsibility gaps. If a human is part of an AI system such as through an \many{} setup, it may be easier to directly link the impact of the AI with the actions of the HITL because the human may have approved the AI's output. By contrast, it has been claimed that systems without a HITL open up a complex web of distributed responsibility, where a large number of parties may share moral responsibility~\cite[p. 194]{sienknecht2024proxy}. In reality, as we show, the link between moral responsibility gaps and HITLs is far more complex, and ultimately is dependent on the type of HITL setup deployed.

In an \turing{} setup, it becomes immensely complex to determine what inputs actually influenced the output of the AI system because of the entanglement between the HITL and the AI. As discussed previously, there's a computational trade-off whereby more powerful reductions with greater human interaction are less predictable than weaker ones. Even if interaction logs are kept to trace the queries and back-and-forth interactions, it may not be possible to evaluate the impact of the HITL's input on the output of the AI due to the indeterminism of the computation tree. Each human input changes what the AI does next, and each AI query changes how the human views the process and thus how they might answer. It may become impossible to discern how and where failures arise and what these features are attributable to. By contrast, it could be a relatively simple task to attribute the role of a HITL with a setup where a human is only at the start and end of the loop (essentially, \many{}), because the human effectively makes a binary decision at the start as to whether to use an AI, and a decision at the end whether to make use of its output and if so, how. 

As such, there is essentially an unavoidable trade-off: when a HITL has greater computational impact on the AI system, it is the case that they are more effectively able to influence the computation by inputting useful information and ``steering'' the AI, having a potentially positive impact. However, this leads to a loss of explainability about the role of the HITL in the system, and in particular, the output of the system. Responsibility gaps emerge as a result of this, where the identification of the points of system failure and the corresponding attribution of responsibility becomes substantially more complex. This unavoidable trade-off between responsibility and explainability, whereby having a better understanding of one necessarily comes at the price of understanding the other, needs careful consideration when using legal responsibility as a tool to motivate the building of better AI systems, as the two can operate at cross purposes.

\subsection{Alternative responsibility mechanisms}

The GDPR and EU AI Act go some way to resolve this issue by imposing liability on the data controller or technology provider to ensure that AI systems are \textit{designed in ways} that enable `meaningful' or `effective' oversight to allow HITLs to safeguard the rights of decision subjects. This is an inherent forward-looking approach, imposing design requirements in order to prevent future harm. However, it is less clear how other legal frameworks might respond to this `responsibility gap' envisaged in \turing{} setups. 

In negligence law\footnote{The tort of negligence deals with cases where someone's carelessness or failure to act reasonably causes harm or loss to another.}, the UK courts have previously had to depart from established principles in challenging cases involving `responsibility gaps' to ensure that  individuals are compensated when they have been harmed but the cause of injury cannot be discerned. This line of cases involves workers developing deadly mesothelioma from exposure to asbestos fibres~\cite{Barker.2006}. Claimants worked for several employers, thus making it difficult to know which employer should be held liable because an individual's exposure can be triggered by a single fibre at any point in time in their various placements. In these cases where it is medically impossible to pinpoint which employer exposed the claimant to the asbestos fibre(s) that caused the mesothelioma, the court held that all the employers could be \textit{jointly liable} if it could be proven that they `materially increased the risk of harm'. The court calculated liability by an amount relative to the the proportion of exposure the claimant had at that employer – despite the fact that they might not have actually caused any harm\footnote{If a claimant worked at one employer for 30\% of their `total exposure time', that employer was liable for 30\% of the damages.}. 

We witness similar responsibility gaps in HITL cases. Here, we suggest that where there are failures from HITL setups, we should be cautious about assigning liability to the HITL even if this might seem most reasonable intuitively - after all, they often have the final control over the system. However, as we have illustrated previously, failures often occur from issues that the HITL has limited control over (see our HITL failure modes). To the authors' knowledge, cases involving HITL failures have not been tested in the EU or UK courts yet, however, in the US, we have already seen an unprincipled tendency to hold HITLs liable for the failures of AI systems~\cite{stamp2024reckless}.  In the previously mentioned US case involving an Uber self-driving car that resulted in a fatal pedestrian accident, the human operator faced all criminal liability even though it was proven that Uber failed to act on safety flaws relating to its the technology~\cite{stamp2024reckless}.

The authors are apprehensive about holding individual HITLs solely liable in the event of failure across all computational setups discussed in this manuscript (\trivial{}, \many{}, and \turing{} setups).\footnote{Unless the HITL has acted in ways that can be proved as deliberately malicious or seriously negligent. But even then, systems designers are responsible for implementing controls that prevent HITL malevolence and create failsafes and checks on how HITLs interact with the system.} Even in entangled \turing{s}, where responsibility is more complicated to assign, the HITL should not be used as a `scapegoat' to protect companies from addressing their contributions to failures. It is beyond the scope of this manuscript to consider how negligence and  criminal law in the EU and UK might exactly operate in these context-sensitive situations, however we support a more nuanced approach to these cases (for example perhaps following similar lines to mesothelioma cases). This is even more salient considering the onerous responsibilities (to safeguard `fundamental rights', `legitimate interests' and `health and safety') that could be required of HITLs in contexts when AI systems are error prone, biased, and frequently act in unexpected ways. 



\section{Conclusion and Suggestions}

In this manuscript, we have demonstrated that different HITL setups can be characterised by a variety of computational reductions. However, as our taxonomy of HITL failure modes highlights, a purely computational overview of HITL does not tell the whole story: HITL setups involve complex sociotechnical decisions and are susceptible to failures beyond human control, which necessitates a new perspective for designing effective and responsible HITL setups. Our legal analysis connected these configurations and failure mechanisms to existing limitations and oversights in the law. This allowed us to make suggestions for more refined rules surrounding HITL requirements, as well as identify a trade-off between legal responsibility attribution and AI technical explainability, and recommend that courts cautiously approach liability in these cases.

Based on this, we make the following suggestions for those either designing or regulating HITL setups:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Define the computational HITL type being sought. If possible, demonstrate more than \trivial{}.
    \item Avoid ``bolting-on'' a HITL to existing workflows; they must be properly integrated into the process.
    \item Establish guidelines for meaningful and effective human oversight that consider different HITL setups.
    \item Ensure that the expectations placed on humans within HITL setups are commensurate with their competency. 
    \item Put in place active measures to protect the human from being the ``moral crumple zone'' protecting the AI.
    \item Understand the trade-offs between legal clarity and technical explainability, to inform more nuanced approaches to assigning liability in HITL failure cases.
\end{enumerate}

If done poorly, a HITL setup can create a dangerous two-way deferral of responsibility between the AI and the human. The human may overly defer to the AI computation, and the AI designers may have overly relied on the human to ensure safety. This combined ``social loafing'' can have disastrous consequences. Integrating a HITL is not a binary process; many possibilities exist, with different consequences. As a bad HITL setup may be just as harmful as no HITL, achieving a \textit{good} setup needs to be the objective.

title: The Cognate Data Bottleneck in Language Phylogenetics
summary:
To fully exploit the potential of computational phylogenetic methods for
cognate data one needs to leverage specific (complex) models an machine
learning-based techniques. However, both approaches require datasets that are
substantially larger than the manually collected cognate data currently
available. To the best of our knowledge, there exists no feasible approach to
automatically generate larger cognate datasets. We substantiate this claim by
automatically extracting datasets from BabelNet, a large multilingual
encyclopedic dictionary. We demonstrate that phylogenetic inferences on the
respective character matrices yield trees that are largely inconsistent with
the established gold standard ground truth trees. We also discuss why we
consider it as being unlikely to be able to extract more suitable character
matrices from other multilingual resources. Phylogenetic data analysis
approaches that require larger datasets can therefore not be applied to cognate
data. Thus, it remains an open question how, and if these computational
approaches can be applied in historical linguistics.

title: Non-spectrality of some piecewise smooth curves and unions of line segments
summary:
We develop a systematic study about the spectrality of measures supported on
piecewise smooth curves by studying the support of the tempered distributions
arising from the tiling equation of some singular spectral measures. In doing
so, we show that the arc-length measures of all closed polygonal lines are not
spectral. {In particular, the boundary of a square is not spectral. We also
show that the ``plus space'' (two crossing line segments) is not spectral.}
Furthermore, our theory also shows that the arc length measures on {smooth}
convex curves with finitely many transverse self-intersections are not
spectral. Finally, several natural open questions about the spectrality of
singular measures and {piecewise} smooth curves will also be discussed.

title: Comparing lifetime and annual fitness measures reveals differences in selection outcomes
summary:
Selection analyses of long-term field data frequently use annual comparisons
from longlived species with overlapping generations to measure fitness
differences with respect to phenotypic characteristics, such as annual
phenological timing. An alternative approach applies lifetime estimates of
fitness that encompass several annual events. We studied selection on emergence
date from hibernation in male and female Columbian ground squirrels,
Urocitellus columbianus (Ord 1915). From 32 years of records, we estimated
lifetime fitness using either lifetime reproductive success (LRS) or matrix
methods, and estimated annual fitness from individual yearly survival and
reproduction. We also modified estimates to statistically control for changes
in mean population fitness over the lives of individuals. We regressed lifetime
fitness metrics on dates of emergence from hibernation, to quantify the
strength of selection on emergence date (a heritable trait). All fitness
metrics were highly correlated, but differences became apparent when estimating
selection coefficients for emergence dates. The annual fitness metric and LRS
produced lower effect sizes of selection coefficients than matrix-based
lifetime fitness and a lifespan approach based on average annual fitness.
Further, only these last two metrics revealed stabilizing selection. These
results suggest that the choice of a fitness metric may influence our
conclusions about natural selection.

title: DeepQuark: deep-neural-network approach to multiquark bound states
summary:
For the first time, we implement the deep-neural-network-based variational
Monte Carlo approach for the multiquark bound states, whose complexity
surpasses that of electron or nucleon systems due to strong SU(3) color
interactions. We design a novel and high-efficiency architecture, DeepQuark, to
address the unique challenges in multiquark systems such as stronger
correlations, extra discrete quantum numbers, and intractable confinement
interaction. Our method demonstrates competitive performance with
state-of-the-art approaches, including diffusion Monte Carlo and Gaussian
expansion method, in the nucleon, doubly heavy tetraquark, and fully heavy
tetraquark systems. Notably, it outperforms existing calculations for
pentaquarks, exemplified by the triply heavy pentaquark. For the nucleon, we
successfully incorporate three-body flux-tube confinement interactions without
additional computational costs. In tetraquark systems, we consistently describe
hadronic molecule $T_{cc}$ and compact tetraquark $T_{bb}$ with an unbiased
form of wave function ansatz. In the pentaquark sector, we obtain weakly bound
$\bar D^*\Xi_{cc}^*$ molecule $P_{cc\bar c}(5715)$ with $S=\frac{5}{2}$ and its
bottom partner $P_{bb\bar b}(15569)$. They can be viewed as the analogs of the
molecular $T_{cc}$. We recommend experimental search of $P_{cc\bar c}(5715)$ in
the D-wave $J/\psi \Lambda_c$ channel. DeepQuark holds great promise for
extension to larger multiquark systems, overcoming the computational barriers
in conventional methods. It also serves as a powerful framework for exploring
confining mechanism beyond two-body interactions in multiquark states, which
may offer valuable insights into nonperturbative QCD and general many-body
physics.

title: Quantum-inspired algorithm for simulating viral response
summary:
Understanding the properties of biological systems is an exciting avenue for
applying advanced approaches to solving corresponding computational tasks. A
specific class of problems that arises in the resolution of biological
challenges is optimization. In this work, we present the results of a
proof-of-concept study that applies a quantum-inspired optimization algorithm
to simulate a viral response. We formulate an Ising-type model to describe the
patterns of gene activity in host responses. Reducing the problem to the Ising
form allows the use of available quantum and quantum-inspired optimization
tools. We demonstrate the application of a quantum-inspired optimization
algorithm to this problem. Our study paves the way for exploring the full
potential of quantum and quantum-inspired optimization tools in biological
applications.

bib.abstract: Development of statistical methods has become very necessary for large-scale correlation analysis in the current “omic” data. We propose ranking analysis of correlation coefficients (RAC) based on transforming correlation matrix into correlation vector and conducting a “locally ranking” strategy that significantly reduces computational complexity and load. RAC gives estimation of null correlation distribution and an estimator of false discovery rate (FDR) for finding gene pairs of being correlated in expressions obtained by comparison between the ranked observed correlation coefficients and the ranked estimated ones at a given threshold level. The simulated and real data show that the estimated null correlation distribution is exactly the same with the true one and the FDR estimator works well in various scenarios. By applying our RAC, in the null dataset, no gene pairs were found but, in the human cancer dataset, 837 gene pairs were found to have positively correlated expression variations at FDR≤5%. RAC performs well in multiple conditions (classes), each with 3 or more replicate observations.

bib.abstract: Pathway analysis, including nontopology-based (non-TB) and topology-based (TB) methods, is widely used to interpret the biological phenomena underlying differences in expression data between two phenotypes. By considering dependencies and interactions between genes, TB methods usually perform better than non-TB methods in identifying pathways that include closely relevant or directly causative genes for a given phenotype. However, most TB methods may be limited by incomplete pathway data used as the reference network or by difficulties in selecting appropriate reference networks for different research topics. Here, we propose a gene set correlation enrichment analysis method, Gscore, based on an expression dataset-derived coexpression network to examine whether a differentially expressed gene (DEG) list (or each of its DEGs) is associated with a known gene set. Gscore is better able to identify target pathways in 89 human disease expression datasets than eight other state-of-the-art methods and offers insight into how disease-wide and pathway-wide associations reflect clinical outcomes. When applied to RNA-seq data from COVID-19-related cells and patient samples, Gscore provided a means for studying how DEGs are implicated in COVID-19-related pathways. In summary, Gscore offers a powerful analytical approach for annotating individual DEGs, DEG lists, and genome-wide expression profiles based on existing biological knowledge.

bib.abstract: DNA damage and genome instability in host cells are introduced by many viruses during their life cycles. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs) manipulation of DNA damage response (DDR) is an important area of research that is still understudied. Elucidation of the direct and indirect interactions between SARS-CoVs and DDR not only provides important insights into how the viruses exploit DDR pathways in host cells but also contributes to our understanding of their pathogenicity. Here, we present the known interactions of both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 with DDR pathways of the host cells, to further understand the consequences of infection on genome integrity. Since this area of research is in its early stages, we try to connect the unlinked dots to speculate and propose different consequences on DDR mechanisms. This review provides new research scopes that can be further investigated in vitro and in vivo, opening new avenues for the development of anti-SARS-CoV-2 drugs.

bib.abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the causative virus for the current global pandemic known as coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). SARS-CoV-2 belongs to the family of single-stranded RNA viruses known as coronaviruses, including the MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV that cause Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), respectively. These coronaviruses are associated in the way that they cause mild to severe upper respiratory tract illness. This study has used an unbiased analysis of publicly available gene expression datasets from Gene Expression Omnibus to understand the shared and unique transcriptional signatures of human lung epithelial cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 relative to MERS-CoV or SARS-CoV. A major goal was to discover unique cellular responses to SARS-CoV-2 among these three coronaviruses. Analyzing differentially expressed genes (DEGs) shared by the three datasets led to a set of 17 genes, suggesting the lower expression of genes related to acute inflammatory response (TNF, IL32, IL1A, CXCL1, and CXCL3) in SARS-CoV-2. This subdued transcriptional response to SARS-CoV-2 may cause prolonged viral replication, leading to severe lung damage. Downstream analysis of unique DEGs of SARS-CoV-2 infection revealed changes in genes related to apoptosis (NRP1, FOXO1, TP53INP1, CSF2, and NLRP1), coagulation (F3, PROS1, ITGB3, and TFPI2), and vascular function (VAV3, TYMP, TCF4, and NR2F2), which may contribute to more systemic cardiovascular complications of COVID-19 than MERS and SARS. The study has uncovered a novel set of transcriptomic signatures unique to SARS-CoV-2 infection and shared by three coronaviruses, which may guide the initial efforts in the development of prognostic or therapeutic tools for COVID-19.

bib.title: Gene Network Analysis of the Transcriptome Impact of SARS-CoV-2 Interacting MicroRNAs in COVID-19 Disease
bib.author: Alexandra Ioana Moatar and Aimee Rodica Chis and Catalin Marian and Ioan-Ovidiu Sirbu
bib.abstract: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), as of June 2022, over 536 million confirmed COVID-19 disease cases and over 6.3 million deaths had been globally reported. COVID-19 is a multiorgan disease involving multiple intricated pathological mechanisms translated into clinical, biochemical, and molecular changes, including microRNAs. MicroRNAs are essential post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, being involved in the modulation of most biological processes. In this study, we characterized the biological impact of SARS-CoV-2 interacting microRNAs differentially expressed in COVID-19 disease by analyzing their impact on five distinct tissue transcriptomes. To this end, we identified the microRNAs’ predicted targets within the list of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in tissues affected by high loads of SARS-CoV-2 virus. Next, we submitted the tissue-specific lists of the predicted microRNA-targeted DEGs to gene network functional enrichment analysis. Our data show that the upregulated microRNAs control processes such as mitochondrial respiration and cytokine and cell surface receptor signaling pathways in the heart, lymph node, and kidneys. In contrast, downregulated microRNAs are primarily involved in processes related to the mitotic cell cycle in the heart, lung, and kidneys. Our study provides the first exploratory, systematic look into the biological impact of the microRNAs associated with COVID-19, providing a new perspective for understanding its multiorgan physiopathology.

bib.title: In silico analysis of SARS-CoV-2 genomes: Insights from SARS encoded non-coding RNAs
bib.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
bib.author: Neha Periwal and Urvashi Bhardwaj and Sankritya Sarma and Pooja Arora and Vikas Sood
bib.abstract: The recent pandemic caused by Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 has resulted in enormous deaths around the world. Clues from genomic sequences of parent and their mutants can be obtained to understand the evolving pathogenesis of this virus. Apart from the viral proteins, virus-encoded microRNAs (miRNAs) have been shown to play a vital role in regulating viral pathogenesis. Thus we sought to investigate the miRNAs encoded by SARS-CoV-2, its mutants, and the host. Here, we present the results obtained using a dual approach i.e (i) identifying host-encoded miRNAs that might regulate viral pathogenesis and (ii) identifying viral-encoded miRNAs that might regulate host cell signaling pathways and aid in viral pathogenesis. Analysis utilizing the first approach resulted in the identification of ten host-encoded miRNAs that could target the SARS, SARS-CoV-2, and its mutants. Interestingly our analysis revealed that there is a significantly higher number of host miRNAs that could target the SARS-CoV-2 genome as compared to the SARS reference genome. Results from the second approach resulted in the identification of a set of virus-encoded miRNAs which might regulate host signaling pathways. Our analysis further identified a similar “GA” rich motif in the SARS-CoV-2 and its mutant genomes that was shown to play a vital role in lung pathogenesis during severe SARS infections. In summary, we have identified human and virus-encoded miRNAs that might regulate the pathogenesis of SARS coronaviruses and describe similar non-coding RNA sequences in SARS-CoV-2 that were shown to regulate SARS-induced lung pathology in mice.
